title: Λύκοι καὶ κύνες ⟨ἀλλήλοις πολεμοῦντες⟩
titleEn: The Wolves and the Dogs at War with One Another
part: The Wolves and the Dogs at War with One Another (Chambry 215 · Perry 343)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 215 (= Perry 343). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκοις καὶ κυσὶν ἦν ποτε ἔχθρα.
sentences.tr: Lykois kai kysin ēn pote echthra.
sentences.l: To wolves and dogs there was once enmity.
sentences.i: There was once enmity between wolves and dogs.
sentences.n: The dative of possession: Greek says "there was to them" where English says "they had". You will meet it constantly. ἔχθρα is not mere dislike but declared hostility — the state of feud that the next lines turn into a campaign.

sentences.t: Κύων δὲ Ἕλλην ᾑρέθη στρατηγὸς κυσίν.
sentences.tr: Kyōn de Hellēn hēirethē stratēgos kysin.
sentences.l: And a Greek dog was-chosen general for the dogs.
sentences.n: ᾑρέθη is the aorist passive of αἱρέομαι in its political sense, "was elected" — the dogs conduct their war on the Athenian model, choosing a στρατηγός. Ἕλλην marks him as a Greek dog; the speech that follows turns on exactly that, the dogs being of many different countries where the wolves are of one stock.

sentences.t: Οὗτος πρὸς τὴν μάχην ἐβράδυνεν· οἱ δὲ λύκοι ἠπείλουν σφοδρῶς.
sentences.tr: Houtos pros tēn machēn ebradynen· hoi de lykoi ēpeiloun sphodrōs.
sentences.l: This one was-slow toward the battle; and the wolves were-threatening violently.
sentences.i: He was slow to give battle, while the wolves threatened fiercely.
sentences.n: Both verbs are imperfect: not one delay and one threat but a state of affairs going on, the general holding back and the enemy loud outside.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· « Οἴδατε τίνος χάριν βραδύνω ; πρέπον ἐστὶν ἀεὶ προβουλεύεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ho de eipen· « Oidate tinos charin bradynō ; prepon estin aei probouleuesthai.
sentences.l: And he said: « Do you know for the sake of what I am slow? It is fitting always to take-counsel-beforehand.
sentences.i: And he said: « Do you know why I hold back? It is always right to plan ahead.
sentences.n: τίνος χάριν, "for the sake of what", is the ordinary Greek for "why". πρέπον ἐστίν is impersonal and takes the infinitive. Chambry prints a space before the Greek question mark, which is his house style throughout. The speech opened here with « runs on to the end of the fable's body; the closing » comes only at the last sentence.

sentences.t: Ὑμῶν γὰρ τὸ γένος καὶ ἡ χροιὰ πάντων ἕν ἐστιν· οἱ ἡμέτεροι δὲ ἐκ πολλῶν τρόπων εἰσὶ καὶ τοῖς τόποις καυχῶνται.
sentences.tr: Hymōn gar to genos kai hē chroia pantōn hen estin· hoi hēmeteroi de ek pollōn tropōn eisi kai tois topois kauchōntai.
sentences.l: For your race and the colour of you all is one; but ours are out of many sorts and boast in their regions.
sentences.i: For your stock and your colour are all one and the same, while ours come of many kinds and take pride each in his own country.
sentences.n: πάντων is a genitive with ὑμῶν, "of you all", and ἕν is a neuter singular predicate covering both subjects together. τρόπος here is "sort, kind" rather than "manner". καυχάομαι takes the dative of what one boasts in.

sentences.t: Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ χροιὰ πάντων οὐκ ἔστι μία καὶ ἴση, ἀλλ’ οἱ μὲν μέλανες, οἱ δὲ πυρροί, οἱ δὲ λευκοὶ καὶ τεφρώδεις.
sentences.tr: Alla kai hē chroia pantōn ouk esti mia kai isē, all’ hoi men melanes, hoi de pyrroi, hoi de leukoi kai tephrōdeis.
sentences.l: But the colour too of all is not one and the same, but some are black, others tawny-red, others white and ash-coloured.
sentences.i: And their colour is not all one and the same either: some are black, some red, some white or ashen.
sentences.n: πάντων here is the dogs, not the wolves: the general is still contrasting his own side with theirs. οἱ μέν … οἱ δέ … οἱ δέ is the standard partition, "some … others … others"; you will meet μέν answered by δέ on nearly every page. πυρρός is flame-coloured, the reddish-tan of a hound's coat.

sentences.t: Καὶ πῶς ἂν δυνηθείην εἰς πόλεμον ἄρχειν τῶν ἀσυμφώνων καὶ μὴ ὅμοια πάντα ἐχόντων ; »
sentences.tr: Kai pōs an dynētheiēn eis polemon archein tōn asymphōnōn kai mē homoia panta echontōn ; »
sentences.l: And how could I be able to command for war those who are out-of-tune and who have not all things alike? »
sentences.i: And how could I command in war creatures so out of tune with one another, who are not alike in everything? »
sentences.n: The optative with ἄν is the potential, the tentative "could I" — a question that expects no. ἄρχω takes the genitive of those commanded. ἀσύμφωνος is a word out of music, "not sounding together", discordant; μή with the participle makes the description generic, the sort of creature they are rather than a report on these ones.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἐν μιᾷ βουλῇ καὶ γνώμῃ πάντων τῶν στρατευμάτων ὄντων κατὰ τῶν ἐναντίων νίκην ποιοῦνται.
sentences.tr: Hoti en miāi boulēi kai gnōmēi pantōn tōn strateumatōn ontōn kata tōn enantiōn nikēn poiountai.
sentences.l: That, all the forces being of one counsel and one mind, they win victory over their adversaries.
sentences.i: The story shows that when all the forces are of one counsel and one mind, they win the victory over their adversaries.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. The condition is carried by a genitive absolute, πάντων τῶν στρατευμάτων ὄντων. νίκην ποιοῦνται is middle, "make a victory for themselves" — the regular periphrasis for winning one.
